name: mint cilantro skillet
instructions:
TWO VARIANTS on the priya-krishna mint-cilantro herb-finish pattern — chicken or tofu cooked in ghee with a warming spice-crust, finished with a raw or lightly-mashed mint + cilantro + garlic + ginger + lime herb mash off heat. See [[jaffrey-lentils]] for the sister recipe by herb pair — same mint+cilantro finish but built on a completely different structural pattern (madhur jaffrey tarka-style dal).

=== VARIANT A — CHICKEN (PRIYA KRISHNA) ===

INGREDIENTS:
- chicken breast (thigh works but breast is preferred — see notes)
- turmeric, chili powder, cumin, ground coriander
- ghee (canonical fat)
- salt

HERB FINISH INGREDIENTS:
- fresh cilantro
- fresh mint
- garlic
- ginger
- lime

PROCEDURE:
1. Cook chicken breast in ghee with turmeric, chili powder, cumin, and coriander until done.
2. Meanwhile, prepare the herb finish (see HERB FINISH TECHNIQUE below — mash/chop-in-pan is the default; mortar-pestle also works; chimichurri as a side option).
3. If using the mash-in-pan approach: chop or mash cilantro, mint, garlic, ginger, and lime, then add to the pan with the cooked chicken at the very end. Toss briefly off heat.
4. If using chimichurri: plate the chicken, serve mint-cilantro-chimichurri on bread or naan on the side.

=== VARIANT B — TOFU ===

INGREDIENTS:
- firm tofu, sliced AS THIN AS POSSIBLE (see notes)
- ghee (canonical fat — see notes on ghee-not-vegetable-oil)
- turmeric, chili powder, cumin, ground coriander
- salt
- (optional) starch (potato or corn) — only if pressing the tofu, for a crispy exterior

HERB FINISH INGREDIENTS:
- fresh cilantro
- fresh mint
- garlic
- ginger
- lime

PROCEDURE:
1. Slice the tofu as thin as you can (a knife or a sharp mandoline both work). Either PRESS (to remove water) or BOIL briefly (~5 min in salted water then pat dry). Both are acceptable prep paths.
2. If pressed: toss the slices in a light dusting of starch. This gives a crispy exterior when pan-cooked. Skip if you boiled.
3. Pan-cook the tofu slices in ghee with turmeric, chili powder, cumin, and coriander until golden on both sides. Use ghee generously — the ghee is doing the flavor work in this variant. Do NOT add vegetable oil (or minimize it if you must).
4. Herb finish: same as chicken variant — mash-in-pan is the default. Chimichurri on bread/naan on the side is also fine.
notes:
Priya-krishna-style mint-cilantro herb finish on a spice-cooked protein. Chicken (variant A) and tofu (variant B) share the pattern: bloom-in-ghee spice-crust on the protein, then the mint+cilantro+garlic+ginger+lime herb mash goes on at the END, never cooked in.

The lentil version (madhur jaffrey tarka-style dal) has been split out into its own recipe — see [[jaffrey-lentils]]. Same herb pair (mint + cilantro) but a completely different technique family (tarka-style dal vs mortar-pestle-herb-on-protein).

DO NOT COOK THE HERBS IN: this is the key technique across both variants. Treating these like a mole and cooking the herb mash into a sauce makes the herbs lose flavor and turns the oil an unappetizing green. The herb component is applied at the end, off heat or just barely warm.

=== HERB FINISH TECHNIQUE ===

MASH OR CHOP AND ADD TO THE PAN IS THE DEFAULT (LIKE A SAAG DISH): the best all-purpose herb finish is to just chop or mash the cilantro + mint + garlic + ginger + lime and add it to the pan at the very end (off heat). This is the same move a saag curry makes — coarsely chopped or lightly mashed fresh herbs folded in raw at the finish. Fast, no separate condiment to make, no serving-vessel considerations. This should be your first choice.

MORTAR-PESTLE MASH — PESTO-STYLE (MY PREFERRED REFINEMENT, NOT PRIYA'S ORIGINAL): pounding cilantro + mint + garlic + ginger + lime in a mortar produces a slightly more integrated paste with released oils and a smoother mouthfeel than chopping does. Treat it like a pesto — pounded into a rough paste, spooned on top at the end. Worth the mortar pull for that specific refinement; the chop-in-pan default gets you 90% of the way there with less work.

PRIYA KRISHNA'S ORIGINAL VERSION IS A BLENDER MARINADE — I DON'T LIKE IT AS MUCH: for the record: Priya Krishna's original technique doesn't mash the herbs like a pesto. She blends them smooth in a blender and uses the result as a marinade for the chicken before cooking. This works — it's the source recipe — but I don't prefer it. The blender-and-marinade approach cooks the herbs into the protein (some of the marinade is on the surface as it hits the pan), which fights the don't-cook-the-herbs rule that makes both variants taste bright and green. Marinated-then-cooked chicken loses the mint-and-cilantro-forward finish that the mash-at-the-end approach preserves. If you're a Priya loyalist go for the marinade; my strong recommendation is the mash-in-pan or mortar-pesto finish instead.

CHIMICHURRI AS A SIDE OPTION — OK BUT NOT PREFERRED, AND ONLY IF SERVED ON BREAD/NAAN: [[mint-cilantro-chimichurri]] (variant A there — indian, with lime and ginger) works alongside either variant, but ONLY as a side condiment served on bread or naan — not spooned directly onto the protein. The chimichurri is a raw allium + vinegar condiment; putting it directly on the pan-cooked chicken or tofu makes the plate read as two dishes (indian pan-cook + argentinian-shape condiment), whereas on bread it functions as a separate scoopable thing that doesn't compete with the primary flavor axis. Preferred order: mash-in-pan > mortar-pestle > chimichurri-on-bread. Skip chimichurri entirely if you don't have bread/naan on the side.

=== VARIANT A NOTES (CHICKEN) ===

CHICKEN BREAST OVER THIGH: priya krishna's recipe works better with chicken breast than thigh. Breast carries the spice-and-herb register cleanly; thigh's fattiness competes with the bright herb finish.

=== VARIANT B NOTES (TOFU) ===

SLICE THE TOFU AS THIN AS POSSIBLE: thin slices are what make this variant work. A knife or sharp mandoline both work — the goal is slices thin enough that the spices penetrate the tofu quickly and the surface-area-to-volume ratio favors flavor development. Thick slabs read as bland-tofu-with-spice-crust rather than fully-flavored tofu.

PRESS OR BOIL — BOTH ARE FINE: two acceptable water-removal paths.
- PRESS: 15-20 min under weight, patted dry. Denser texture. If pressed, you can toss the slices in a light dusting of starch (potato or corn) before pan-cooking to get a crispy exterior.
- BOIL: brief ~5 min boil in salted water, then pat dry. The surface protein sets and drives out water; slices hold together well in the pan. No starch coating with the boiled path.
Both work; the choice comes down to whether you want the crispy-starch-crust texture (press + starch) or the softer-inside texture (boil).

GHEE IS THE CANONICAL FAT — DON'T USE VEGETABLE OIL: flavor in this variant is built mostly from ghee. Use ghee generously; the browned tofu picks up nutty ghee character that vegetable oil can't provide. Do NOT add vegetable oil — or minimize it aggressively if you must (say, to boost the smoke point). This is unlike a lot of indian pan-cooking where vegetable oil + ghee is a fine blend; here the tofu-plus-ghee-alone is the point.

=== SHARED CROSS-VARIANT NOTES ===

KASHMIRI CHILI POWDER AND RED CHILI FLAKES ARE BOTH NECESSARY — SAME RULE AS PALAK PANEER (SEE PESTLE-SAAG-CURRY): the indian chile stack for this dish is generic chili powder + kashmiri chili powder + red chili flakes. Each does a different job:
- KASHMIRI CHILI POWDER: brings bright red color and gentle warming heat without aggression. This is what makes the finished dish visually indian rather than reading as generic pan-cooked-meat-with-herbs. Non-optional.
- RED CHILI FLAKES: the whole-form chile presence — scattered on the pan-cook for a heat-and-visual accent.
- GENERIC CHILI POWDER: covers the broad heat + earthy character.
Same rule holds in the palak paneer branches (see [[indian-saag-curry]]) — the indian chile stack there wants the same kashmiri + flakes + generic combination for the same reasons.

=== JALAPEÑOS OR SERRANOS FOR FRESH HEAT ===

A small amount of fresh green chile adds a bright, whole-form heat that the powdered chile stack doesn't provide. Works for both variants.

- SERRANOS ARE PREFERABLE — slit lengthwise (1-2 slits per pepper) so the heat leeches out without the whole chile dissolving into the dish. Slit-whole rather than diced; you can fish them out at the end if you want less heat, or leave them in.
- JALAPEÑOS also work — but DICE them (they're bigger and don't leech evenly if left whole). USE SPARINGLY — 1/4 of a jalapeño or less for the whole recipe. Jalapeños are cheap; don't be afraid to toss the rest of the pepper.

Don't overshoot either way — the point is a background heat that lifts the dish, not a chile-forward register. If in doubt, err less.

=== BELL PEPPERS ARE CLASHING ===

Bell peppers (any color) don't fit this dish. Their sweet-vegetal character fights the herb-forward mint + cilantro register and pushes the plate toward a generic pan-cook stir-fry look. The green chile slot above is what handles pepper in this recipe; bell peppers are the wrong direction. Marked clashing.

=== SERVING PAIRING — [[braised-turnips]] AS A SIDE (ESPECIALLY WITH LEMON OR LIME JUICE) ===

[[braised-turnips]] pairs particularly well with either variant of this dish as a vegetable side. The dense root-vegetable braise sits cleanly against the herb-forward register of the mint-cilantro-skillet — the register-fit is right (mild, buttery/ghee, savory) and neither dish crowds the other on the plate.

ESPECIALLY WITH LEMON OR LIME JUICE added to the turnips at the glaze stage — the citrus finish on the braised roots picks up and echoes the lime in the herb mash, tying the plate together. A squeeze of lime over the turnips right when the glaze reduces takes them from a generic braised root into an intentional pairing.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[jaffrey-lentils]]: the split-out lentil sister recipe. Same mint + cilantro herb finish but built on a completely different structural pattern (madhur jaffrey tarka-style dal — whole spices bloomed in vegetable oil, onion+garlic+tomato base, whole green lentils simmered, herbs stirred in raw at the end). Same herb pair, different technique family.
- [[mint-cilantro-chimichurri]]: raw mint+cilantro chimichurri (variant A — indian). Optional side condiment on bread/naan, per the note above.
- [[indian-saag-curry]]: shares the kashmiri+chili-powder+red-chili-flakes stack (see SHARED CROSS-VARIANT NOTES).
